explanations.title: Simvastatin + Clarithromycin
explanations.explanation: Clarithromycin is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor that markedly raises simvastatin exposure, which increases the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. This combination is contraindicated and should be escalated for prescriber review before the next dose. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Sildenafil + Isosorbide mononitrate
explanations.explanation: Sildenafil and isosorbide mononitrate both increase nitric-oxide/cGMP signalling and cause vasodilation, so taking them together can produce severe, potentially fatal hypotension. This combination is contraindicated and should be reviewed by the prescriber. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Warfarin + Ibuprofen
explanations.explanation: Warfarin and ibuprofen together increase the risk of serious bleeding, especially gastrointestinal bleeding. This occurs because NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and injure the gastric mucosa, adding to warfarin's antihaemostatic effect. The patient is taking both medications, so this additive bleeding risk is directly relevant. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Oxycodone + Diazepam
explanations.explanation: Oxycodone and diazepam both depress the central nervous system and respiratory drive, so their combined use can produce additive CNS and respiratory depression, with the potential for profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death (FDA boxed warning). This is directly relevant because the patient is taking both agents concurrently. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Methotrexate + Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole)
explanations.explanation: This patient is taking both methotrexate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole), a combination that can cause serious bone-marrow suppression (pancytopenia). The risk arises because both drugs are antifolates and trimethoprim reduces methotrexate clearance, increasing methotrexate exposure. Given the critical severity, the clinician should review whether this combination is appropriate for this patient. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Digoxin + Amiodarone
explanations.explanation: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein, which raises digoxin levels and can lead to digoxin toxicity (nausea, arrhythmia, bradycardia). This patient takes both digoxin and amiodarone, so the risk of elevated digoxin levels is directly relevant. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Digoxin + Furosemide
explanations.explanation: Furosemide, a loop diuretic, can cause hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, which increases sensitivity to digoxin toxicity. This patient takes both digoxin and furosemide, so monitoring potassium, magnesium, and digoxin level is relevant. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Verapamil + Metoprolol
explanations.explanation: Verapamil and metoprolol both slow the heart and reduce cardiac contractility, so their combined use can produce additive negative chronotropic and inotropic effects. This raises the risk of bradycardia, AV block, hypotension, and heart failure in this patient. The combination therefore warrants close monitoring. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Lithium + Ibuprofen
explanations.explanation: Ibuprofen (an NSAID) can reduce renal lithium clearance, which may raise lithium levels and lead to toxicity. Because this patient takes both lithium and ibuprofen, the clinician should review whether lithium levels need close monitoring or whether the NSAID should be avoided. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Lithium + Lisinopril
explanations.explanation: Lisinopril (an ACE inhibitor) can reduce renal lithium clearance, which may raise lithium levels and lead to toxicity. Since this patient takes both lithium and lisinopril, the clinician should review whether lithium levels need close monitoring. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Ibuprofen + Lisinopril
explanations.explanation: Ibuprofen (an NSAID) can reduce renal prostaglandins and blunt the antihypertensive effect of lisinopril, potentially reducing blood-pressure control and increasing the risk of kidney injury. Because this patient takes both ibuprofen and lisinopril, the clinician should consider monitoring blood pressure and kidney function, and review whether long-term NSAID use is appropriate. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Citalopram + Amiodarone
explanations.explanation: Citalopram and amiodarone both prolong the QT interval, and their combined use produces additive QT-interval prolongation that raises the risk of torsades de pointes. This is relevant because the patient is taking both medications concurrently. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Simvastatin + Amlodipine
explanations.explanation: Amlodipine weakly inhibits CYP3A4, which raises simvastatin exposure and increases the risk of myopathy, particularly at higher simvastatin doses. Because this patient is taking both simvastatin and amlodipine, the clinician should review whether the simvastatin dose is appropriate, as the label limits simvastatin to 20 mg/day when used with amlodipine. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Clopidogrel + Omeprazole
explanations.explanation: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which reduces the formation of clopidogrel's active metabolite and thereby diminishes clopidogrel's antiplatelet effect. This is relevant because the patient is taking both clopidogrel and omeprazole, so the intended antiplatelet benefit of clopidogrel may be reduced. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Spironolactone + Potassium chloride
explanations.explanation: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic, and adding a potassium chloride supplement creates a risk of serious hyperkalaemia because both raise potassium levels. This patient is taking both agents, so the combination warrants review. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Spironolactone + Ramipril
explanations.explanation: Spironolactone and ramipril both reduce potassium excretion, so their combined use raises the risk of hyperkalaemia, particularly if kidney function is reduced. This patient is taking both drugs, making potassium and kidney function monitoring relevant. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Potassium chloride + Ramipril
explanations.explanation: Ramipril, an ACE inhibitor, reduces potassium excretion, and combining it with a potassium chloride supplement increases the risk of hyperkalaemia. This patient is taking both, so confirming whether the supplement is still needed and monitoring potassium are relevant considerations. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Sertraline + Naproxen
explanations.explanation: Sertraline (an SSRI) impairs platelet function while naproxen (an NSAID) injures the gastric mucosa, so the combination increases the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in this patient. The clinician should consider gastroprotection or an alternative analgesic. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Atorvastatin + Colchicine
explanations.explanation: Atorvastatin and colchicine can both cause muscle toxicity, and their combined use has been associated with reports of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis, likely through additive muscle toxicity. For this patient taking both agents, monitoring for muscle pain or weakness is warranted. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Triple whammy: Losartan, Hydrochlorothiazide, Diclofenac
explanations.explanation: This combination of an ARB (Losartan), a diuretic (Hydrochlorothiazide), and an NSAID (Diclofenac) markedly increases the risk of acute kidney injury. The patient is taking all three agents, so this triple-whammy risk applies directly to them. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Losartan + Diclofenac
explanations.explanation: Diclofenac can reduce renal prostaglandins, blunting the antihypertensive effect of Losartan and raising the risk of kidney injury. Because the patient takes both Losartan and Diclofenac, blood-pressure control and kidney function may be affected. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Anticoagulant + antiplatelet + NSAID: Warfarin, Clopidogrel, Naproxen
explanations.explanation: This patient is taking three medications that each impair haemostasis: warfarin (an anticoagulant), clopidogrel (an antiplatelet), and naproxen (an NSAID). The combined antihaemostatic effect produces a very high risk of major bleeding, so this combination warrants escalation for prescriber review before the next dose. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Warfarin + Clopidogrel
explanations.explanation: Warfarin and clopidogrel act through additive antihaemostatic mechanisms (anticoagulant plus antiplatelet), increasing the risk of major bleeding in this patient who is taking both. The clinician should review whether the combined therapy is indicated and its planned duration. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Warfarin + Naproxen
explanations.explanation: Warfarin and naproxen together increase the risk of serious bleeding, particularly gastrointestinal bleeding, because NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and injure the gastric mucosa on top of warfarin's anticoagulant effect. The clinician should review whether the NSAID is necessary and, if continued, monitor INR and signs of bleeding and consider gastroprotection. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Clopidogrel + Naproxen
explanations.explanation: Clopidogrel and naproxen have an additive antihaemostatic effect combined with GI mucosal injury, increasing the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding in this patient taking both. The clinician should consider whether the NSAID is necessary and whether gastroprotection is warranted. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Two or more strongly anticholinergic drugs: Oxybutynin, Diphenhydramine, Amitriptyline
explanations.explanation: This patient is taking three medications with strong anticholinergic activity (oxybutynin, diphenhydramine, and amitriptyline), and their combined effect produces a cumulative anticholinergic burden. This accumulation increases the risk of confusion, delirium, constipation, and urinary retention in older adults. Given the patient's age of 80, the clinician should review whether each of these anticholinergic drugs is still needed. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Three or more CNS-active drugs: Sertraline, Zolpidem, Gabapentin
explanations.explanation: This patient is taking three CNS-active drugs (sertraline, zolpidem, and gabapentin), which together increase the risk of falls and fractures in older adults. The additive CNS-depressant effects of these agents raise the likelihood of sedation, dizziness, and impaired balance. Given the patient's age of 78, this combination warrants review to consider whether the number of CNS-active drugs can be reduced. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Aspirin (low dose) + Sertraline
explanations.explanation: Aspirin (low dose) and sertraline both impair platelet function, and their combined use produces an additive effect that increases the risk of bleeding. This is relevant because the patient is taking both agents concurrently. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Therapeutic duplication: Ibuprofen, Naproxen
explanations.explanation: This patient is taking two NSAIDs, ibuprofen and naproxen, which belong to the same drug class. Taking more than one NSAID at the same time adds to the risk of gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney injury without providing additional benefit. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Therapeutic duplication: Warfarin, Apixaban
explanations.explanation: This patient is prescribed both Warfarin and Apixaban, two anticoagulants from the same therapeutic group. Taking two anticoagulants together greatly increases the risk of major bleeding. The clinician should review whether more than one drug from this group is intended. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Therapeutic duplication: Ibuprofen
explanations.explanation: Ibuprofen appears more than once in this patient's medication list, which creates a risk of double dosing and an unintentionally higher total dose of the same drug. This is relevant because the patient's list contains Ibuprofen listed twice, so the clinician should confirm whether both entries are intended or represent a duplicate. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Warfarin + Aspirin (low dose)
explanations.explanation: Warfarin (an anticoagulant) and low-dose aspirin (an antiplatelet) have an additive antihaemostatic effect, which increases the risk of major bleeding. This is relevant because the patient is taking both medications together. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Apixaban + Naproxen
explanations.explanation: Apixaban and naproxen both impair haemostasis, and their combined use produces an additive antihaemostatic effect that increases the risk of bleeding. This is relevant because the patient is taking both agents concurrently. Supported by the interaction database only.

explanations.title: Warfarin + Aspirin (low dose)
explanations.explanation: Warfarin and low-dose aspirin together increase the risk of major bleeding through an additive antihaemostatic effect, combining an antiplatelet agent with an anticoagulant. This is relevant because the patient is taking both medications, so the clinician should review whether combined therapy has a clear indication and monitor for bleeding. Supported by the interaction database only.
